blogs.title: Digital Inclusion of Women through Self-Help Groups: What the Literature has to Say
blogs.excerpt: Self-help groups have become a key route for women's digital and financial inclusion in rural India. This piece surveys the literature on current initiatives, scaling barriers, and the behavioural questions that still need attention.
blogs.contentMarkdown:
## Introduction

At the rural level, initiatives that aspire for digital financial inclusion of women often involve Self Help Groups. This is a strategic way to accomplish female digital inclusion and financial literacy of women. When we examine the literature on digital financial inclusion at the level of Village Organisations, two key factors must be mentioned. First, the digital documentation of financial services and databases; and second, the facilitation of digital operations using a variety of channels. These two aspects need to be in accordance with one another as they are interdependent and will help accomplish financial inclusion in a holistic manner. Providing digital literacy at the grassroots level is necessary to avoid information asymmetry or improve access to schemes and the benefits they entail.

## Empowering Initiatives at Present

[Vishalakshi(2026)](https://www.ijcrt.org/papers/IJCRT2602392.pdf) notes that State Governments have made efforts to foster capacity building by using digital tools. For instance, a "Tablet Didi'' project was taken up by the State Livelihood Promotion Society in the districts Ranchi, Pakur, and Western Singhbhum. In this project, members of self-help groups received training on how to operate tablets for accounting, transactions, minutes of meetings, etc. These Didis are native village women who have been given the responsibility of MIS-based web reporting to the relevant areas. They guide women in different groups and inform the women of the various programmes and schemes that they are entitled to. Under this project, a unique application called Sawalekha is also created for these women and is accessible in both Hindi and English. This project highlights that digital literacy transforms women into enterprise owners from subsistence.

[Bhaskaran et al. (2021)](https://www.hindustantimes.com/ht-insight/gender-equality/transforming-the-lives-of-rural-women-through-the-day-national-rural-livelihoods-101629883809951.html) outline a similar effort made in Chhattisgarh by Initiative for What Works to Advance Women and Girls in the Economy (IWWAGE) and Haqdarshak to provide digital access to SHG women. Through this platform, information about the application process, and required documentation for welfare schemes has been provided to SHG women. These efforts made by the non-governmental organisation has caught the attention of the Chhattisgarh State Livelihood Mission (Bihan) as well as other organisations who are now collaborating with IWWAGE to create a suitable digital ecosystem for SHGs operating in different villages.

[Batra et al. (2022)](https://www.inspirajournals.com/uploads/Issues/1324128267.pdf) note a similar effort made by the Haryana Government in 2018 with the help of a private company, Nucleus Software, which has introduced the digital currency tool PaySe where cash is stored as electronic money in the Payse card provided by the company. This initiative was launched in the village of Bighar, Fatehabad district to make transactions cashless. SHGs now employ PaySe digital solutions to carry out digital transactions such as the collection of savings, loan repayment, etc. Kerala has a Shrestha Scheme as well which aims to provide digital services to its SHGs, while some states have gone a step further by providing tools to SHG women themselves. The Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty operating in Andhra Pradesh employs a mobile bookkeeping app where data entry, correction, and information validation are carried out. It is operated by the village mobile bookkeeper who works for the respective Village Organization (VO).

## Factors Inhibiting Digitisation Scaling

Remote SHG digitization attempts across India have proven to be nourishing for SHGs. However, the main hurdle the Government faces in its digitisation efforts is a "phase issue", highlighted by [Scott et al.(2021)](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2021-051193). Although each phase is laid down on paper accurately, achieving these phases is difficult because of resource constraints. The government is unable to equip itself with sufficient manpower to achieve its digitization goals as there is an absence of Government functionaries who can participate in digital capacity building. Understanding and navigating through backend issues that are likely to arise while operating digital tools then becomes a hindering factor. This percolates at the grass-root level and the result is a minimal application of digital tools to educate SHG members about financial or non-financial aspects of their activities. Besides, the authors suggest that reliance on digital platforms might result in the absence of a "human touch." The paper also makes an interesting point about how by employing people who belong to the same community to spread digital literacy, a sense of trust is instilled among SHG members which could make digital literacy a successful venture for the government.

Persistent problems pointed out in the literature centre around [incomplete digital literacy](https://www.ijhssi.org/papers/vol7(11)/Version-1/A0711010105.pdf) in the SHG ecosystem due to which SHG members lose out on the opportunity to equip themselves with digital tools. States also have limited convergence with potential partners to improve the conception of digital literacy or its propagation to self-help groups which causes limited understanding of the benefits of digitisation among ground level functionaries. There is also not a sufficient amount of qualitative research to understand the supply-side constraints experienced by digital transaction service providers or to assess the ["penetration"](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/358667235_Self-Help_Groups_and_COVID-19_Effects_on_and_Challenges_for_the_National_Rural_Livelihoods_Mission_in_India) of these efforts on the socio-economic front of SHG development.

Another thing to keep in mind is that digitization does not solely imply financial services being offered online. It is only made possible if members possess mobile and digital technologies as a medium to facilitate financial transactions. The [World Bank's "Global Findex Database" report of 2021](https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099818107072234182/pdf/IDU06a834fe908933040670a6560f44e3f4d35b7.pdf) also reported that rural Indian women who possessed a bank account were 18% less likely to make digital payments. This may be possible because the informal nature of the rural economy poses a bit of a challenge since cash-based transactions are preferred by the rural population. Besides, since rural residents have limited money-spending habits, an absence of digital infrastructure such as internet access or even smartphones, scepticism of the safety of online transactions does not necessarily instill a need in them to switch to digital transactions.

## Conclusion

The barriers encapsulated by the literature make observations on why there seems to be limited use of digital tools among women on the lines of technical barriers. The social or behavioural aspects that hinder SHG digitization are vital factors. Lack of trust is rightly outlined as a behavioural challenge but it is also necessary to trace the attitude of members' openness to venturing into new modes of conducting business. To put it simply, there is a need to articulate how women with the help of their SHG peers can be motivated to flourish in the digital age. Although the absence of an active state policy with this motive could prove inhibiting, hearing what the grassroots functionaries have to say about switching to digital means of transactions could provide insights into how to accelerate digitization efforts. The discussion in the literature centres around why the Government is unable to achieve digitisation and where it is lacking, but there is not sufficient literature on how the SHGs working with the Government influence how much effort the Government takes to accelerate its attempts. Similarly, how group dynamics affect the motivation members have in using digital tools as an ally needs to be delved into.

blogs.title: Indian Men's Mental Health: A Silent Crisis and Current Solutions
blogs.excerpt: Men's mental health in India remains under-recognized despite its links to suicide, substance use, chronic illness, and lost productivity. This piece examines the scale of the crisis and the interventions already in place.
blogs.contentMarkdown:
## Introduction

Mental health is an indication of a person's psychological and emotional well-being that affects how one perceives and experiences life. Poor mental health in men is an acknowledged problem, but it is challenging to tackle because of the social shame attached to emotionality and the pressure to embody extreme stoicism. Due to this, mental health is under-recognised and underreported in India. Unfortunately, poor mental health often manifests in substance abuse, aggression, and suicide, which should concern us.

## What the Data Demonstrates

Mental health disorders amount to 13.5% in urban areas and 6.9% in rural areas according to the [National Mental Health Survey (NMHS) of 2015-2016](https://indianmhs.nimhans.ac.in/phase1/Docs/Report2.pdf). In 2023, the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) found that men accounted for 72.8% of all suicides.

According to the [National Mental Health Survey (NMHS, 2015-16)](https://indianmhs.nimhans.ac.in/phase1/Docs/Report2.pdf), men exhibit 9.1% alcohol use disorders. Men also have higher prevalence of current and lifetime mental morbidity at 13.9% and 16.7%, resulting in substance use disorders, severe mental disorders, and behavioral disorders. Meanwhile, women have a higher percentage of depression (3.01%) and anxiety (3.69%) disorders, which are also components of mental morbidity. However, male-dominated categories drive up the overall prevalence of mental morbidity.

Poor mental health also has physiological consequences. [Vaccarino et al. (2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12587323/) highlight the strong relationship between mental health disorders and cardiovascular disease. Societal pressure to be the breadwinner, a demanding job ecosystem, escapism, unhealthy coping mechanisms, and a sedentary lifestyle are thus leading to a higher incidence of heart attacks, hypertension, diabetes, and liver diseases in men.

There is a shortage of mental health professionals in the country as well. The [World Health Organization's Mental Health Atlas 2020](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240036703/) highlighted major human-resource gaps in mental healthcare delivery. In this regard, accessibility in rural areas is especially compromised.

The [SMART Mental Health project](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7923507/) partnered with community health workers in 44 primary health care centres (PHCs) across 133 villages in Haryana and Andhra Pradesh to address treatment gaps in mental health services in rural India. Participants in the project admitted that social stigma, lack of privacy, and fear of ridicule discouraged them from seeking professional help. Men from rural Andhra Pradesh and Haryana demonstrated the persistence of this attitude. They are often indifferent to such initiatives as mental health assistance is disorganised, and awareness drives and campaign timings can clash with daily-wage job timings.

## Current Interventions

The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare hosts the toll-free number [14416 / 1-800-891-4416 through Tele-MANAS](https://www.mohfw.gov.in/?q=en%2Fpress-info%2F10197), which provides telephone-based counselling, psychotherapy, psychiatric consultations, and referrals to appropriate professionals in case of urgent care in all Indian states. As of [February 6, 2026](https://www.mohfw.gov.in/?q=en%2Fpress-info%2F10197), Tele-MANAS had also expanded its mobile application and regional-language support further.

For drug and alcohol addiction problems, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has launched the [Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan toll-free number 14446](https://socialjustice.gov.in/common/47564). It functions in a similar manner and provides rehabilitation support, community awareness drives, and district-level campaigning activities. Correspondingly, the Ministry of Home Affairs hosts the [National Narcotics Helpline MANAS number 1933](https://narcoticsindia.nic.in/pressrelease/180724.pdf), which targets drug trafficking, illicit cultivation, and related offences. Citizens can use this toll-free number to report suspicious activity or seek help.

While there are around [1.78 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2152534&lang=2&reg=3) providing integrated diagnostic, preventive, and curative services for physical as well as mental health issues, targeted efforts that address personnel limitations also exist. Some Community Mental Health Competence (CMHC) efforts tackling social stigma have emerged in states such as Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, and Chennai. Such efforts bring change gradually but remain essential.

Additionally, to address the physiological effects of poor mental health, the Government launched the [Fit India Movement](https://fitindia.gov.in/about) in 2019 to promote community-based fitness activities. This initiative encourages simple lifestyle changes like walking, exercising, and mindful eating in civil society. Such an initiative benefits the cause since studies have shown that [exercise can help regulate stress responses involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25462913/).

## Conclusion

The policy ecosystem currently needs to target inequality in accessibility to mental health helplines, shortage of professionals, and stigma. As per the NFHS-5 survey, men constitute around 51.56% of India's population, over 70% of the workforce, and dominate crucial fields. An economy and society can only prosper when its citizens are productive, feel safe, and are optimistic about the nation's future.

For good mental health, building resilience, maintaining emotional regulation, and healthy communication are vital. If men are struggling to do so, interventions that promote access to available resources are necessary. When men embrace their individuality and address their struggles in a healthy manner, they can become better co-workers, friends, husbands, fathers, and fellow citizens, uplifting the community. Therefore, fixing men's mental health is important.

blogs.title: Gender Issues: Understanding Gender and Society
blogs.excerpt: Gender shapes expectations, access, safety, and opportunity across education, work, media, and identity. Understanding these dynamics helps build a more just and compassionate society for everyone.
blogs.contentMarkdown:
Understanding Gender and Society

Gender is one of the first labels assigned to us. Before we speak our first word, before we take our first step, our society begins shaping expectations around who we are supposed to be. From the colours we wear, to the careers we choose. Gender influences not only how others perceive us but also how we perceive ourselves.

While progress has been made over the past couple of years to address inequality, gender issues remain deeply rooted in our social structures, cultural norms and personal experiences.

Understanding gender issues is not about creating a comparison between men and women. It is about recognizing how rigid expectations, unequal opportunities and systemic biases affect people differently in various aspects of life and how we can work together to build a more just and compassionate society.

## Sex vs. Gender: The Difference

Before we move further, we must understand the terms to get a better insight. Many people use the terms sex and gender interchangeably but they are not the same.

Biological sex refers to physical characteristics such as chromosomes, hormones and anatomy of an individual. On the other hand, gender is a social and cultural construct. It involves roles, behaviours, expectations and identities that societies assign to each individual.

For centuries, societies operated within a binary framework male and female, assigning strict roles to each. Men were often expected to be strong, dominant and financially responsible, while women were expected to be nurturing, emotional and primarily responsible for domestic work.

These roles may have provided structure in traditional societies but they also limited individual freedom and potential.

## Barriers to Growth: Education and Workplace Inequality

One of the most visible gender issues worldwide is inequality in access to education and employment opportunities.

In many parts of the world, girls still face problems in schools due to poverty, cultural norms, lack of sanitation facilities, early marriage or safety concerns. Without education, their opportunities to achieve financial independence reduce dramatically.

Even in societies where women have access to education, workplace inequality persists. The gender pay gap remains one of the persisting global issues, with women often earning less than men for similar roles and responsibilities.

Be it leadership positions in politics, business, arts or science, they are still dominated by men.

At the same time, gender expectations also harm men. Many boys grow up being told not to cry, not to show vulnerability and to equate masculinity with emotional suppression. This pressure can lead to mental health struggles that often go unaddressed for years.

## Gender-Based Violence: A Global Concern

Gender based violence is one of the most serious and urgent issues globally.

Women and girls are affected by domestic violence, harassment and sexual assault. Fear of violence often restricts freedom, influencing where someone feels safe to travel, what they wear and how they behave in public.

Addressing gender based violence requires more than laws. It demands cultural change, teaching respect, consent and equality from an early age.

Similarly, men can also be victims of violence, though societal stigma often prevents them from speaking up. Breaking the silence around these issues is essential for true gender justice.

## Media and Reinforcement of Gender Norms

The media plays a powerful role in shaping gender norms. Movies, advertisements, music and social media frequently reinforce stereotypes where women may be portrayed primarily through their appearance, while men are portrayed as powerful decision-makers.

Such portrayals subtly influence how young people see themselves and what they believe they are capable of achieving.

There is no doubt the media also has the power to challenge stereotypes. Stories that depict women as leaders, men as caregivers and individuals expressing diverse gender identities help normalize a broader spectrum of human experience.

Representation matters because it expands the horizon.

## Gender Identity and Evolving Conversations

In the past couple of years, conversations about gender identity have become more visible. Some individuals do not identify strictly as male or female. For them, rigid gender systems can be restrictive and harmful.

While perspectives on gender identity can vary across cultures and belief systems, one principle remains universal: every human being deserves dignity and respect.

Regardless of personal views, fostering dialogue grounded in empathy rather than hostility creates healthier communities.

Gender issues are not always dramatic or headline-making. Sometimes they are subtle in everyday conversations, expectations and experiences.

Why are girls often praised for being quiet and well-behaved, while boys are excused for being naturally mischievous? Why are women asked about balancing family and career in interviews more frequently than men? Why is caregiving still primarily seen as a woman’s responsibility?

These are small biases that have built over time. They influence confidence, ambition and opportunity. Challenging them requires awareness and highlighting that such assumptions are based not on ability, but on gender.

## Towards an Equal Society

Real change begins with education. Schools, families and communities play a critical role in shaping perspectives. Teaching young people about equality, mutual respect and shared responsibility lays the foundation for a more balanced society.

Open conversations are equally important. When people share experiences we must listen actively and seek understanding rather than argue. Through dialogue growth becomes possible.

Gender equality is not a women’s issue or a men’s issue. It is a human issue.

Gender issues are complex, deeply rooted and interconnected with culture, economics, religion and history. But at their core, they revolve around one simple principle: being just.

When individuals are free to pursue education, careers, relationships and self-expression without being limited by rigid expectations, society as a whole benefits. Innovation increases, families grow healthier, and communities become stronger.

Addressing gender issues is not about replacing one dominance with another. It is about balance, recognizing the value, dignity and potential of every person.

blogs.title: Women and Equity in AI Technology
blogs.excerpt: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is reshaping economies and societies. This piece examines equity in AI, the gendered digital divide, and the steps needed to build inclusive, safe, and fair technology systems.
blogs.contentMarkdown:
The world finds itself at the threshold of the Fourth Industrial Revolution characterised by [velocity, scope, and systems impact.](https://www.weforum.org/stories/2016/01/the-fourth-industrial-revolution-what-it-means-and-how-to-respond/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=22228224717&gbraid=0AAAAAoVy5F4vZIO7zLrAjqdSREJe1x4RT&gclid=CjwKCAiA-__MBhAKEiwASBmsBDIHKgRbK5Sgbmo3ilKggSp2rKafgDVKqLnQmw-_zIZdAAE8eY3gGBoCXTsQAvD_BwE) Technological innovations are changing the world as we know it faster than ever before. Emerging technologies like artificial intelligence, robotics, 3-D printing, nanotechnology, biotechnology and quantum computing, etc. are changing the rules of businesses and societies. What does it mean for the women in those businesses and societies?

## Equity in Technological Solutions

Equity in technology can be defined as [intentional design, development, deployment, and governance of technology systems](https://climate.sustainability-directory.com/term/equity-in-technology/) to ensure values such as justice, fairness and inclusion for all.

The percentage of women in STEM is a matter of concern. Women have far less access and digital literacy as compared to men. There are [only 35 per cent of students in STEM education.](https://www.un.org/en/un75/impact-digital-technologies) There are [only 22 per cent of jobs in the artificial intelligence (AI) arena.](https://www.un.org/en/un75/impact-digital-technologies) During conception, when a technology is shaped under a narrow perspective, it negatively affects inclusiveness. [OECD found that,](https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/gender-equality-and-digital-transformation.html#:~:text=Human%20capital%20is%20required%20to,encouraged%20to%20undertake%20STEM%20studies.) male bias in ICT reduces the inclusiveness in digital transformation. It also found that while the exposure to AI remains the same for both males and females in their occupations, women are significantly under-represented in occupations that have the highest exposure to AI technology.

## Barriers- Gatekeeping of Technology?

A major barrier to inclusion of women in technology related fields are gender based digital divide, early age discouragement and stereotyping of job roles, limited role models in STEM, [lack of mentorship,](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388221838_The_Intersection_of_Gender_and_Technology_Implications_for_Workplace_Relations) gender bias and [discrimination in hiring](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388221838_The_Intersection_of_Gender_and_Technology_Implications_for_Workplace_Relations) and [an unwelcoming and hostile environment for women](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388221838_The_Intersection_of_Gender_and_Technology_Implications_for_Workplace_Relations) in technology spaces. These factors inhibit women from being part of the workforce in technology related fields.

## What Next?

Attention must be redirected to the consequences of the Fourth Industrial Revolution on people and more specifically on women. A major dissuader of the usage of technology is the possible abuse and harassment on digital platforms; therefore, it is imperative to ensure safety on these platforms. Enforcing strict laws to ensure privacy and timely action against harassment along with providing digital literacy to women can foster a safer digital environment for women.

Focus needs to be drawn upon the unequal access to technology due to barriers such as income, education, region, social status, etc. Addressing these differences is key to bringing change. One way to address this is by reexamining existing knowledge about technology as a government provided public good. Governments must ensure an [inclusive approach in skilling](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2024/12/algorithm-and-eve_0e889c45/full-report.html#a1zLan24) women in artificial intelligence technology.

It is also the need of the hour to promote inclusion of women in the field of STEM and in workplaces with high AI exposure. Mandating diversity in hiring and promoting skills-first approach in hiring and other targeted approaches can address discrimination in hiring. Awareness campaigns can be run to illustrate the importance of access to technology to women. With these changes there can be significant progress in achieving equity in the AI workforce.

blogs.title: Climate Fueled Gender Violence: Can the Solutions be Nudged?
blogs.excerpt: Climate stressors can amplify inequality and violence. This piece looks at evidence on climate-fueled gender-based violence and explores behavioural change approaches alongside traditional policy tools.
blogs.contentMarkdown:
A concern flagged by the United Nations (UN) over two years ago, climate change fueled gender violence needs to be given another look. Repeated emphasis is placed on the need for gender equity to tackle climate change. While there are some widely acknowledged solutions to the issues, such as stricter laws and the Duluth Model, can there be a behavioural approach?

[Baschieri et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%22Baschieri%20A%22%5BAuthor%5D) (2025) mention that climate change leads to food insecurity and adverse effects on livelihoods. Increased income inequality as a result of climate change and stress caused by extreme heat, beyond its impact on the surrounding environment, has ripple effects on [gender based violence](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%22Baschieri%20A%22%5BAuthor%5D). Climate change is bound to increase inequalities and food insecurity. This increasing inequality may lead to greater tension in interpersonal dynamics.

It was found that the [rise in intimate partner femicide can increase up to 28% during heatwaves.](https://www.spotlightinitiative.org/publications/colliding-crises-how-climate-crisis-fuels-gender-based-violence) These stressors can lead to increase in gender based violence in the form of "psychosocial abuse, physical violence, sexual violence, coercion, survival sex, child marriage, female genital mutilation, selective malnourishment, and even femicide." It has been found that [every 1°C rise in temperature is associated with a 4.7 per cent rise in violence](https://www.unicef.org/eap/media/20741/file/Gender%20Policy%20Brief%20-%20Gender-Based%20Violence%20and%20Climate%20Crisis.pdf.pdf) caused by a sexually intimate partner termed as intimate partner violence (IPV). [By 2090 at a 2°C rise in temperature an additional 40 million women and girls will experience IPV.](https://www.unicef.org/eap/media/20741/file/Gender%20Policy%20Brief%20-%20Gender-Based%20Violence%20and%20Climate%20Crisis.pdf.pdf)

Despite awareness on the issues, the [UN Spotlight Initiative brief (2025)](https://www.spotlightinitiative.org/publications/colliding-crises-how-climate-crisis-fuels-gender-based-violence) found how only 0.04% of the climate-related development assistance focuses on gender equality. ["Climate action must incorporate a gender lens to elevate the unique needs of women to avoid these harms"](https://www.spotlightinitiative.org/publications/colliding-crises-how-climate-crisis-fuels-gender-based-violence). What can be done?

There is a recognised need for gender based financing, data collection on the impact of climate change for women and protective measures against gender based violence. Several countries have pledged to focus on gender equality and have started initiatives to tackle the issue at hand. Strict enforcement of laws, improved access to help, campaigning for creating awareness, providing education to women and income opportunities are some of the commonly recommended solutions.

One of the widely acknowledged methods is the [Duluth Model](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1359178907000353) from the feminist approach which speaks of educating men on violence. However many studies have rendered it ineffective.

[Gilchrist et al.(2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8551949/) in their study provided an eight step behavioural change wheel utilising the COM-B Framework. Localised solutions to gender violence can be formulated using this method.

In the case of climate change fueled violence, the problem can be identified as the stress caused by climate change and growing inequality. The targeted change in behaviour can be the release of stress through violence. Focus can be put on providing alternate means to release mental strain. Community support groups, promotion of collective activities, [promoting self regulation and crisis management](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8551949/) and access to mental healthcare can be some ways to channelise the stress.

Greater efforts are required to understand climate change caused gender violence. More data and research is required in this area. Moreover it is imperative to formulate a joint effort of using traditional policy tools along with behavioural change efforts that can lead to improved outcomes. Transfer of knowledge is also a necessity of the hour to ensure that proven models regarding the issues can be replicated across the world.
